USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture without new escalation or concession. The existing $250B tariff coverage and the scheduled January 1 rise from 10% to 25% on List 3 already exert significant leverage. Allow that pressure to work while keeping the door open for talks. Do not announce new tariffs before the midterms, but do not roll anything back either — the strategic position favors the US.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of -0.3 reflects a position of relative US advantage. China is running out of retaliatory capacity: its latest response covered only $60B of US goods at reduced rates of 5-10%, down from the 25% matching it used on earlier rounds (CNN, Sept 19). Capital Economics noted China 'has been unable to match the US dollar-for-dollar.' Meanwhile the US still has a $267B tariff threat in reserve that would cover virtually all remaining Chinese exports. US macro data shows an economy absorbing the trade shock well: consumer sentiment at 100.1 (UMich Sept 2018), industrial production at 104.1 (Aug 2018), and unemployment near historic lows. The dollar has strengthened ~5.5% over six months (DTWEXBGS), reflecting capital flows into US assets.

However, the position is not costless. Soybean farmers face devastating losses — prices down ~$1.90/bu vs Brazilian competitors, Chinese orders down 80% year-over-year (farmdoc daily, Sept 10). The USDA's $12B aid package (announced Aug 27) is a stopgap, not a solution, and farm-state senators are restless ahead of November midterms. Corporate bond spreads (Baa) have widened ~31bp to 4.9%, suggesting some credit stress.

The action score of 0.0 (hold) is justified by several factors: (1) List 3 just took effect on Sept 24 — its full impact hasn't been felt yet, and adding more tariffs now would increase uncertainty without clear strategic gain; (2) the scheduled Jan 1 step-up to 25% is a built-in escalation lever that can be used as a negotiating deadline; (3) China has not yet canceled trade talks entirely — Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang said the new tariffs 'brought uncertainty' but stopped short of pulling out (Politico, Sept 18); Kudlow publicly invited renewed talks on Sept 12; (4) midterms are 5 weeks away, and further escalation risks alienating farm-state voters without proportionate gain; (5) as Arthur Kroeber of Gavekal noted, the principal objective may be 'to force US multinational companies to pull back their investments in China' — that structural shift is already underway and doesn't require additional tariff rounds. The right play is strategic patience: hold what we have, let the Jan 1 deadline create pressure, and see if Beijing sends Liu He to Washington.

US macro economy holding strong: consumer sentiment 100.1, industrial production growing, dollar up 5.5%
Soybean farmers facing severe losses (prices down ~1/3, China orders down 80% YoY)

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5-10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
Consumer sentiment: 100.1 (Sept 2018), up from 96.2 in Aug. Change +1.3 over 6 months.
Industrial Production: 104.1 (Sept 2018), up from 103.3 in April. Steady growth.
Broad Dollar Index: 113.67 (Sept 26), up from 107.70 in April. +5.5% appreciation.
Capital Economics: 'China has been unable to match the US dollar-for-dollar in this round of tariffs.' CNN notes China's retaliatory rates fell to 5-10% vs previous 25% matching.
Price gap between Brazilian and US soybeans reached $1.90/bushel. Sales to China down 80% year-over-year as of August 30.
NPR: Soybean cash prices fallen by as much as a third. Orders from China have stopped coming in.

Standard Chartered's Ding Shuang: 'There is still chance for talks before the White House increases tariffs to 25%, but Trump doesn't seem to want any serious negotiation with Beijing before the U.S. midterm elections.'

Arthur Kroeber (Gavekal): 'The principal objective of the tariffs is probably not to bring Beijing to the bargaining table. Rather, it is to force US multinational companies to pull back their investments in China.'
